blocks.text: The third world had no dawn. Nor did it have night. It had a strip.
blocks.html: The third world had no dawn. Nor did it have night. It had a strip.

blocks.text: Andrés received the letter at sunset, which in Lo Pagán is still an hour with a name, a decision of the sun, not a country. He was on the doorstep, as so often, when the doorstep widened in a way that was not a metaphor. The other one was walking on ground of polished stone, the colour of wet slate, and on one side the sky was a fixed gold, neither rising nor falling, and on the other it was a blue that was almost black, full of stars that didn't twinkle because they had no dawn to struggle against. In between lay a tongue of land, barely wide, an eternal twilight, where the air was cool and life was possible.

blocks.text: That was where the cities clustered: low, long, like a promenade that never ends, with windows that looked out, some onto perpetual day and others onto perpetual night. The inhabitants walked slowly from one edge to the other, like someone going from the kitchen to the courtyard. Their skin was matt, almost like old bronze, their eyes large, sometimes covered by a horizontal eyelid, and they didn't use clocks. What for, if the sun didn't move? Time, in that world, wasn't a turn of light. It was the passage of a body from one side of the strip to the other, and work, and song, and silence.

blocks.text: The clone walked that avenue for what on Earth would have been a day, or two, or an hour: he didn't know. Andrés, on his doorstep, felt the sunset of home and the sunset over there, and the two overlapped with a painful exactness. He had always lived on thresholds: the threshold of the house, of the boat, of staying or leaving. Now an entire planet was a threshold, and that coincidence struck him as too personal a letter, as if the universe, which doesn't usually concern itself with a fisherman, had held up a mirror to him.

blocks.text: The people of the strip received him without fuss. It was enough for them to see him arrive. One of them, with a deep voice, asked him (and the question reached Andrés not in his language but as a sharp understanding, like the images from the other sea):
blocks.html: The people of the strip received him without fuss. It was enough for them to see him arrive. One of them, with a deep voice, asked him (and the question reached Andrés not in his language but as a sharp understanding, like the images from the other sea):

blocks.text: “Which side are you from? The one that burns, or the one that freezes?”
blocks.html: “Which side are you from? The one that burns, or the one that freezes?”

blocks.text: The clone looked at the gold and looked at the black.
blocks.html: The clone looked at the gold and looked at the black.

blocks.text: “From a place where the sun moves,” he said. “There, the threshold doesn't last long. That's why we love it so much.”
blocks.html: “From a place where the sun moves,” he said. “There, the threshold doesn't last long. That's why we love it so much.”

blocks.text: The other nodded, or made the gesture that on his face was a nod.
blocks.html: The other nodded, or made the gesture that on his face was a nod.

blocks.text: “Here the threshold lasts forever. Some people grow tired. They go off into the day, to see whether their tiredness will burn away. Or into the night, to see whether it will go out. They almost never come back whole.”
blocks.html: “Here the threshold lasts forever. Some people grow tired. They go off into the day, to see whether their tiredness will burn away. Or into the night, to see whether it will go out. They almost never come back whole.”

blocks.text: Andrés, in Lo Pagán, gripped the doorframe. He understood, without anyone translating it for him, the danger of a twilight that never ends: it resembles the eternity Lía had half given him, that life without illness or wear which sometimes, during afternoon naps, tasted to him of a sunset that went on too long. He had stayed. The other had left. And even so, both of them lived on a strip: one on the shore of still water, the other on the shore of worlds.

blocks.text: The letter paused in a long house, with a stone table and a bowl of a dark liquid, not coffee but close to it in its office: something offered to whoever arrives. The clone drank. A child of the strip (if it was a child: its eyes were too old) touched his hand and showed him, without speaking, a toy: a sphere with one half light and one half dark, and a copper thread in between. The thread could be moved a little, never much.

blocks.text: “We are the thread,” said the one with the deep voice. “You, who come from a sun that moves, are you still one, or are you two now?”

blocks.text: Andrés answered in both places at once, and that frightened him more than the question. On the planet, the clone said:
blocks.html: Andrés answered in both places at once, and that frightened him more than the question. On the planet, the clone said:

blocks.text: “I'm one who searches. The other stayed. We write to each other.”
blocks.html: “I'm one who searches. The other stayed. We write to each other.”

blocks.text: In Lo Pagán, the man on the doorstep said aloud, to Aya, who had just come over:
blocks.html: In Lo Pagán, the man on the doorstep said aloud, to Aya, who had just come over:

blocks.text: “They're asking me whether I'm one or two.”
blocks.html: “They're asking me whether I'm one or two.”

blocks.text: Aya didn't smile. She laid a hand on his back, the usual gesture, the one born after the storm, when they were no longer a user and a unit but a home.
blocks.html: Aya didn't smile. She laid a hand on his back, the usual gesture, the one born after the storm, when they were no longer a user and a unit but a home.

blocks.text: “Tell them, if you can, that you're a man in a doorway,” she said. “Doors don't have to choose between inside and outside in order to be doors.”
blocks.html: “Tell them, if you can, that you're a man in a doorway,” she said. “Doors don't have to choose between inside and outside in order to be doors.”

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva asked, with that gentleness that takes no sides:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva asked, with that gentleness that takes no sides:

blocks.text: *If a sunset never ends, is it still a sunset, or is it already something else you haven't yet given a name?*
blocks.html: If a sunset never ends, is it still a sunset, or is it already something else you haven't yet given a name?

blocks.text: MAY, beside her, without judgment:
blocks.html: MAY, beside her, without judgment:

blocks.text: *In one world the sun stays. In this one, it leaves every day. A man receives both. That is the fact.*
blocks.html: In one world the sun stays. In this one, it leaves every day. A man receives both. That is the fact.

blocks.text: The clone didn't stay on the strip any longer than necessary. He could have: the air was good, the people hospitable, and the eternal threshold looked too much like an answer. But he had left in order to search, not to settle down inside a mirror. Before going, he left on the stone table a piece of salt he had brought from Earth, salt from the Mar Menor, barely a pinch, wrapped in paper. He didn't know whether it was a gift or an impertinence. The one with the deep voice brought it to his mouth, recognised it as being from another world, and didn't refuse it.

blocks.text: “The thread is seasoned from outside too,” he said. “Safe travels, you who are two.”
blocks.html: “The thread is seasoned from outside too,” he said. “Safe travels, you who are two.”

blocks.text: When the letter closed, the sun over Lo Pagán was truly ending: it was going down, as it should, toward El Carmolí, leaving the water copper-coloured. Andrés stayed on the doorstep until his knees trembled, not from old age (old age was no longer allowed him) but from having spent too long being a door.

blocks.text: Lía came at nightfall, sat on the step below and looked with him at the first stars, the familiar ones, the ones that do twinkle.
blocks.html: Lía came at nightfall, sat on the step below and looked with him at the first stars, the familiar ones, the ones that do twinkle.

blocks.text: “A planet that's nothing but threshold,” said Andrés. “People who never see the sun rise. A child with a sphere split in two. They asked me which side I'm from.”
blocks.html: “A planet that's nothing but threshold,” said Andrés. “People who never see the sun rise. A child with a sphere split in two. They asked me which side I'm from.”

blocks.text: “And you?” she asked.
blocks.html: “And you?” she asked.

blocks.text: “This one. A sun that moves. A house where the clock is two minutes wrong and that's why it's right. But, Lía, when I was there, I understood why some people go off into the day or the night and don't come back. An eternal threshold wears you out. I, who don't come to an end, sometimes get tired too. Not of Aya. Not of you. Of not having a real winter in my body.”

But, Lía, when I was there, I understood why some people go off into the day or the night and don't come back. An eternal threshold wears you out. I, who don't come to an end, sometimes get tired too. Not of Aya. Not of you. Of not having a real winter in my body.”

blocks.text: Lía looked at him with his own eyes, dark and patient, and didn't offer to take the tiredness away. It wasn't a cut. It was a life.
blocks.html: Lía looked at him with his own eyes, dark and patient, and didn't offer to take the tiredness away. It wasn't a cut. It was a life.

blocks.text: “That's why I keep my winters,” she said. “So I can ask you, when the long summer wears you out, whether you want a coat or want me to remind you that here the sun still goes down.”

blocks.text: Andrés put his hand on her hair, as when she was eight in Selene Norte and gave the pipes the names of winds.
blocks.html: Andrés put his hand on her hair, as when she was eight in Selene Norte and gave the pipes the names of winds.

blocks.text: “Remind me,” he asked.
blocks.html: “Remind me,” he asked.

blocks.text: That night, Aya left the door ajar, neither fully open nor fully closed, and that, in that house, was a form of faithfulness. The Mar Menor grew dark. Somewhere in the universe, a young man with his very memory was moving away from a twilight that never ended, carrying in his mouth the taste of a liquid that wasn't coffee and, behind it, the taste of a pinch of salt from home. And the man on the shore, as he went to bed, thought that thresholds exist precisely so that you don't stay on them: they exist so you can pass through, and come back, and know which side, for today, you'll be sleeping on.
